plan: Two passages weighted toward Key Ideas and Details (15 of 20): CLD-P-ACT-R-000074, social science on Kevin Lynch's The Image of the City (1960: Boston, Jersey City, Los Angeles; paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks; imageability; limits of the sample); CLD-P-ACT-R-000075, humanities on kabuki's origins (Izumo no Okuni around 1603 on the Kamo River; the 1629 and 1652 bans; onnagata). Topics checked against both workstreams. Plus a replacement Key Ideas item on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000073 for R072-17, which was withdrawn for cueing by a sibling item. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: The City in the Mind
passages.text:
In the late 1950s, the urban planner Kevin Lynch asked a simple question: when people picture the city they live in, what do they actually see? To find out, he and his colleagues interviewed residents of three American cities, Boston, Jersey City, and Los Angeles. They asked people to describe trips they took regularly and to draw rough maps of their cities from memory. The results, published in 1960 in a book called The Image of the City, have shaped how planners think about cities ever since.

Lynch found that people's mental maps were built from a small number of recurring elements. There were paths, the streets and walkways along which people moved; edges, such as shorelines or railroad tracks, that marked boundaries; districts, areas with a recognizable character; nodes, such as busy intersections and squares, where paths met; and landmarks, distinctive objects that served as points of reference. A good city, in Lynch's view, was one in which these elements were easy to recognize and fit together into a clear whole, a quality he called "imageability."

The three cities differed sharply. Boston residents produced detailed, confident maps, organized around features such as the Charles River, the Common, and the State House dome. Jersey City residents, by contrast, struggled. Many described their city as formless, and when asked to name distinctive features, some pointed to the skyline of Manhattan across the river rather than to anything in Jersey City itself. Los Angeles residents tended to describe the city in terms of the routes they drove, with long stretches that they could barely recall.

Lynch did not claim that a clear image was the only thing that made a city good. But he argued that it mattered more than planners usually admitted. A city that is hard to picture is hard to navigate, and a person who cannot form a mental map of a place, he suggested, may never come to feel at home there.

Later researchers have pointed out the limits of Lynch's study. He interviewed relatively few people, most of them middle class, and a city's image may look very different to a delivery driver, a recent immigrant, or a child. Lynch himself acknowledged some of these limits. Still, his basic insight has proved durable: a city exists not only in its streets and buildings but also in the minds of the people who use it.

passages.title: Riverbank Beginnings
passages.text:
Kabuki, one of the great theatrical traditions of Japan, began not on a stage but on a riverbank. Around 1603, a performer named Izumo no Okuni began presenting dances and comic sketches on the dry bed of the Kamo River in Kyoto. Her troupe, made up largely of women, drew large crowds with flamboyant costumes and scenes from everyday life, and other troupes soon imitated her.

The new entertainment was popular, but the authorities of the Tokugawa shogunate viewed it with suspicion. In 1629, they banned women from performing on the kabuki stage, concerned about the rowdy crowds and the social mixing the performances encouraged. Troupes of young men took their place, but these too were banned in 1652. From then on, kabuki was performed by adult men alone.

It would be easy to see these bans only as a loss, and in one sense they were: the women who had created kabuki were shut out of it for centuries. Yet the restrictions also produced one of kabuki's most admired arts. Actors known as onnagata devoted their careers to playing women's roles, and because they could not rely on simply being women, they built their portrayals out of carefully studied gestures, postures, and ways of speaking. Their art was not an imitation of how women actually behaved so much as a stylized idea of femininity, refined over generations and passed from teacher to student.

Some of the most celebrated actors in kabuki's history were onnagata, and audiences came to value their performances precisely because of their artifice. A great onnagata was admired not for persuading viewers that they were watching a woman but for the skill with which every movement had been shaped.

The story of kabuki's beginnings is thus a reminder that artistic traditions are shaped by forces outside art as well as within it. A government decree intended to control public behavior helped create one of the theater's most distinctive forms, one that has outlasted the government that imposed it.

passages.title: Half Asleep
passages.text:
For most animals, including people, sleep is an all-or-nothing affair: when we fall asleep, both halves of the brain slow down together. But some animals have found a way around this. Dolphins, for example, can rest one half of the brain at a time while the other half stays alert. During this "unihemispheric" sleep, the eye connected to the waking half of the brain typically stays open, and the dolphin keeps swimming and surfacing to breathe.

Birds do something similar. In a 1999 study, the neuroscientist Niels Rattenborg and his colleagues placed mallard ducks in a row and recorded their brain activity as they slept. Ducks in the middle of the row tended to sleep with both halves of the brain at once. Ducks at the ends of the row, however, more often slept with one half of the brain awake, and they tended to keep open the eye facing away from the other ducks, toward the direction from which a predator would most likely approach. The finding suggested that the birds could control which half of the brain stayed alert, depending on where danger was likely to come from.

Some animals change the way they sleep depending on their surroundings. Northern fur seals sleep with both halves of the brain when they rest on land. At sea, however, they mostly use unihemispheric sleep, often floating on one side while paddling with one flipper to keep their nostrils above the water.

The most dramatic example may be the great frigatebird, a seabird that can stay aloft over the ocean for weeks at a time. For years, scientists wondered whether frigatebirds slept in flight at all. In 2016, Rattenborg's team attached small devices that recorded brain activity to frigatebirds in the Galápagos Islands. The birds did sleep while flying, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both, but only in brief bursts that added up to about forty minutes a day. On land, the same birds slept more than twelve hours a day.

These findings raise as many questions as they answer. If half a brain's worth of sleep is enough for a dolphin, researchers wonder, why do other animals, including humans, sleep with the whole brain at once? One possibility is that sleeping with both halves allows the brain to recover more efficiently, so that animals sleep this way whenever it is safe to do so. For now, though, the frigatebird's forty minutes remain a puzzle: no one knows how the birds manage on so little sleep, or what, if anything, it costs them.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that Boston is better designed than any other American city.
choices.B: explain how planners have redesigned Jersey City since the 1950s.
choices.C: describe a study of how people picture cities and assess its influence.
choices.D: compare the driving habits of residents of three large American cities.

candidates.evidence: his basic insight has proved durable
candidates.explanation: The passage presents Lynch's study, its findings, its argument, its limits, and its lasting insight.

A.rationale: The passage reports how Boston residents described their city; it does not rank all cities.

B.rationale: The passage does not discuss later redesigns.

D.rationale: Driving appears only in the description of Los Angeles.

hints: What does the last paragraph conclude about the study?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer must cover the whole passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Lynch and his colleagues gathered information by:

choices.A: interviewing residents and asking them to draw maps from memory.
choices.B: tracking residents' daily movements around the city with recording devices.
choices.C: comparing official city maps with traffic records.
choices.D: surveying city planners about the cities they had designed.

candidates.evidence: draw rough maps of their cities from memory
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says they interviewed residents about regular trips and asked them to draw maps from memory.

B.rationale: The passage mentions interviews and drawings, not tracking devices.

C.rationale: The passage does not mention official maps or traffic records.

D.rationale: The interviews were with residents, not planners.

hints: What did the researchers ask residents to do?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following would Lynch most likely classify as an edge?

choices.A: A busy square where several streets meet
choices.B: A tall clock tower visible from many streets
choices.C: A neighborhood known for its old brick houses
choices.D: A railroad line that separates two neighborhoods

candidates.evidence: edges, such as shorelines or railroad tracks, that marked boundaries
candidates.explanation: Lynch's edges are boundaries such as shorelines or railroad tracks, so a railroad line between neighborhoods is an edge.

A.rationale: A meeting place of paths is a node, not an edge.

B.rationale: A distinctive reference object is a landmark.

C.rationale: An area with a recognizable character is a district.

hints: How does the passage define an edge?

strategy.explanation: Match each choice to one of Lynch's five elements.

candidates.remember: Apply a definition from the passage to a new example.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, the term "imageability" most nearly refers to how easily a city:

choices.A: can be photographed for tourist brochures.
choices.B: can be pictured as a clear and connected whole.
choices.C: can be imagined as it might look in the future.
choices.D: can attract new residents from other places.

candidates.evidence: fit together into a clear whole, a quality he called
candidates.explanation: Lynch defines imageability as the quality of elements that are easy to recognize and fit together into a clear whole.

A.rationale: The term concerns mental images, not photographs.

C.rationale: The term concerns the city as it is, not as it might become.

D.rationale: The passage does not connect imageability to attracting residents.

hints: What does the sentence say the quality consists of?

strategy.explanation: Read the definition just before the term.

candidates.remember: Terms are often defined right before or after they appear.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Jersey City residents differed from Boston residents in that Jersey City residents:

choices.A: had difficulty identifying distinctive features of their own city.
choices.B: produced more detailed maps organized around a river.
choices.C: described their city mainly in terms of the long routes they regularly drove.
choices.D: refused to draw maps of the city where they lived.

candidates.evidence: Many described their city as formless
candidates.explanation: Jersey City residents struggled, called their city formless, and sometimes named features of Manhattan instead.

D.rationale: They struggled; the passage does not say they refused.

hints: What did Jersey City residents point to when asked for distinctive features?

strategy.explanation: Contrast the two groups in paragraph 3.

candidates.remember: Keep track of which details belong to which group.

candidates.stem: The detail that some Jersey City residents named the Manhattan skyline as a distinctive feature mainly suggests that these residents:

choices.A: preferred living in Manhattan to living in Jersey City, across the river.
choices.B: had never visited most parts of Jersey City.
choices.C: considered the skyline part of Jersey City itself.
choices.D: found more to recognize in a neighboring city than in their own.

candidates.evidence: pointed to the skyline of Manhattan across the river rather than to anything in Jersey City itself
candidates.explanation: Naming a skyline across the river shows that the most recognizable feature they could think of lay outside their own city.

A.rationale: The detail concerns what they could picture, not where they wished to live.

B.rationale: The passage gives no information about which areas they had visited.

C.rationale: The passage says they pointed to Manhattan rather than to anything in Jersey City.

hints: Where is the feature they named?

strategy.explanation: Connect the detail to the point about formlessness.

candidates.remember: Inferences should go no further than the evidence.

author_checklist.hardness: must connect the detail to Jersey City's lack of imageability

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 4, Lynch suggested that a person who cannot form a mental map of a place:

choices.A: will eventually move to a different city.
choices.B: can still navigate it easily by following signs.
choices.C: may never come to feel at home there.
choices.D: should be included in the planning of new streets.

candidates.evidence: may never come to feel at home there
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says such a person "may never come to feel at home there."

A.rationale: Lynch does not predict that such people will move.

B.rationale: Lynch says a city that is hard to picture is hard to navigate.

D.rationale: The paragraph does not discuss involving residents in planning.

hints: What does the last sentence of paragraph 4 say?
candidates.remember: Answer from the specific paragraph named.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, one limitation of Lynch's study was that:

choices.A: it examined only cities located along major rivers.
choices.B: it included relatively few people, most of them middle class.
choices.C: it relied on official maps instead of residents' accounts.
choices.D: it was published too late to influence city planners.

candidates.evidence: He interviewed relatively few people, most of them middle class
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 5 notes that Lynch interviewed relatively few people, most of them middle class.

A.rationale: The passage does not identify this as a limitation.

C.rationale: The study relied on residents' accounts.

D.rationale: The passage says it has shaped planning ever since.

hints: What do later researchers point out in paragraph 5?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: The main function of the last paragraph is to:

choices.A: acknowledge weaknesses in the study while affirming its central idea.
choices.B: reject Lynch's conclusions as unsupported by the evidence he gathered.
choices.C: introduce a newer study that replaced Lynch's research on city images.
choices.D: explain how Lynch chose which cities to study.

candidates.evidence: Still, his basic insight has proved durable
candidates.explanation: The paragraph lists limits of the study and then, with "Still," affirms its lasting insight.

B.rationale: The paragraph says his basic insight has proved durable.

D.rationale: The paragraph does not explain how the cities were chosen.

hints: What does "Still" signal in the paragraph?

strategy.explanation: Track the turn in the paragraph.

candidates.remember: A paragraph can concede limits and still affirm a main point.

candidates.stem: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about Lynch's work?

choices.A: Its findings apply equally to every resident of every city in the world.
choices.B: It has had little influence on how planners have thought about cities.
choices.C: It proved that a clear image is all that makes a city good.
choices.D: Its central insight remains valuable even though its sample was limited.

candidates.evidence: his basic insight has proved durable
candidates.explanation: The author describes the study's limits but calls its basic insight durable.

A.rationale: The author notes that a city's image may differ for different people.

B.rationale: The author says it has shaped planners' thinking ever since.

C.rationale: Lynch did not claim this, and the author says so.

hints: What does the author say both about the limits and about the insight?

strategy.explanation: Look for the author's own judgment.

candidates.remember: Separate the author's view from the views the author reports.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Kabuki was invented by government officials who wanted to control the public's behavior.
choices.B: Restrictions imposed on kabuki helped give rise to one of its most distinctive arts.
choices.C: Women's performances were the most admired part of kabuki throughout its history.
choices.D: Onnagata actors aimed to persuade audiences that they were actually women.

candidates.evidence: A government decree intended to control public behavior helped create one of the theater's most distinctive forms
candidates.explanation: The passage traces kabuki's origins, the bans, and the rise of the onnagata, concluding that outside restrictions helped create a distinctive art.

A.rationale: Kabuki began with Okuni's performances; the government restricted it later.

C.rationale: Women were banned from kabuki for centuries.

D.rationale: The passage says they were admired for artifice, not for persuading viewers.

hints: What does the last paragraph say the story shows?

strategy.explanation: Read the conclusion, then check it against each paragraph.

candidates.remember: A main-idea answer must include the passage's conclusion.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Izumo no Okuni first presented her performances:

choices.A: in a theater built for her by the shogunate.
choices.B: in the homes of wealthy families in Edo.
choices.C: on the dry bed of a river in Kyoto.
choices.D: at religious festivals in temples.

candidates.evidence: on the dry bed of the Kamo River in Kyoto
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says she performed on the dry bed of the Kamo River in Kyoto.

A.rationale: The passage says the shogunate viewed kabuki with suspicion.

B.rationale: The passage names Kyoto and a riverbank.

hints: Where does paragraph 1 say she performed?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, which of the following happened first?

choices.A: Women were banned from performing on the kabuki stage.
choices.B: Young men were banned from performing kabuki.
choices.C: Kabuki came to be performed only by adult men.
choices.D: Onnagata became among kabuki's most celebrated actors.

candidates.evidence: In 1629, they banned women from performing on the kabuki stage
candidates.explanation: The ban on women (1629) came before the ban on young men (1652), after which only adult men performed and the onnagata tradition developed.

B.rationale: This happened in 1652, after the 1629 ban on women.

D.rationale: This developed after adult men took over all roles.

hints: Which dates does paragraph 2 give?
candidates.remember: Use dates and sequence words to order events.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the authorities banned women from performing kabuki because they were concerned about:

choices.A: the cost of the troupes' elaborate costumes.
choices.B: competition with older forms of Japanese theater, such as Noh.
choices.C: the quality of the comic sketches that Okuni's troupe performed.
choices.D: the rowdy crowds and social mixing the performances encouraged.

candidates.evidence: concerned about the rowdy crowds and the social mixing the performances encouraged
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives the authorities' concern: rowdy crowds and social mixing.

A.rationale: Costumes are mentioned as a draw, not as a reason for the ban.

B.rationale: Older forms of theater are not mentioned.

C.rationale: The passage does not say the authorities objected to the sketches' quality.

hints: What reason does paragraph 2 give for the ban?
candidates.remember: Distinguish a stated reason from other details nearby.

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that onnagata developed their stylized portrayals partly because they:

choices.A: could not rely on simply being women to portray women.
choices.B: were required by law to exaggerate every gesture.
choices.C: wanted to mock the women who had founded kabuki.
choices.D: had studied the dances performed by Okuni's original troupe.

candidates.evidence: because they could not rely on simply being women
candidates.explanation: The passage says that because they could not rely on simply being women, they built portrayals from studied gestures and speech.

B.rationale: No law about gestures is mentioned.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests mockery; their art was admired and refined.

D.rationale: The passage does not say they studied Okuni's dances.

hints: What does paragraph 3 say about why they studied gestures?
candidates.remember: Look for stated causes behind a development.

author_checklist.hardness: cause embedded in a long sentence

candidates.stem: In paragraph 3, the author's attitude toward the bans is best described as:

choices.A: wholly approving, since in the author's view they improved kabuki.
choices.B: entirely critical, since in the author's view they ruined kabuki.
choices.C: acknowledging their cost while recognizing an unexpected result.
choices.D: uninterested, since the bans had little effect.

candidates.evidence: It would be easy to see these bans only as a loss
candidates.explanation: The author grants that the bans were a loss for women performers but notes that they also produced the onnagata's art.

A.rationale: The author calls the bans a loss in one sense, so the approval is not total.

B.rationale: The author says the bans also produced an admired art.

D.rationale: The author treats the bans as consequential.

hints: What two sides does paragraph 3 present?
candidates.remember: Balanced attitudes are signaled by concessions followed by "yet."

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the art of the onnagata was passed on:

choices.A: through written manuals published by the shogunate.
choices.B: from teacher to student over generations.
choices.C: by observing how women in Kyoto actually behaved.
choices.D: in schools founded by Okuni's original troupe.

candidates.evidence: refined over generations and passed from teacher to student
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the art was refined over generations and passed from teacher to student.

A.rationale: The passage does not mention manuals or the shogunate's involvement in training.

C.rationale: The passage says the art was a stylized idea, not an imitation of actual behavior.

D.rationale: Okuni's troupe is not connected to onnagata training.

hints: What does the end of paragraph 3 say?
candidates.remember: Watch for choices that contradict the passage.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 4, audiences admired great onnagata mainly for:

choices.A: their ability to fool audiences into thinking they were women.
choices.B: their knowledge of kabuki's history and early performers.
choices.C: the comic sketches they added to traditional plays.
choices.D: the skill evident in their carefully shaped movements.

candidates.evidence: for the skill with which every movement had been shaped
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says a great onnagata was admired for the skill with which every movement was shaped.

A.rationale: The passage says they were not admired for persuading viewers of this.

B.rationale: History is not given as a reason for admiration.

C.rationale: Comic sketches are associated with Okuni's early troupe.

hints: What does paragraph 4 contrast?
candidates.remember: A "not X but Y" sentence tells you which reason is correct.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "artifice" most nearly means:

choices.A: skillful craft.
choices.B: clever deception.
choices.C: elaborate costume.
choices.D: playful humor.

candidates.evidence: precisely because of their artifice
candidates.explanation: The next sentence explains that audiences valued the skill with which every movement was shaped, so "artifice" means skillful craft.

B.rationale: The passage says they were not admired for fooling viewers.

C.rationale: The word refers to their performance skills, not their clothing.

hints: What does the following sentence say audiences valued?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Use the surrounding sentences to choose among a word's meanings.

candidates.stem: In the last paragraph, the author suggests that kabuki's history shows that artistic traditions can be shaped by:

choices.A: the personal tastes of individual performers alone.
choices.B: audiences who demand realistic performances.
choices.C: political decisions that were not intended to affect art.
choices.D: rivalries between theater troupes in different cities.

candidates.evidence: A government decree intended to control public behavior
candidates.explanation: The author says forces outside art, such as a decree meant to control behavior, helped create the onnagata tradition.

A.rationale: The author stresses forces outside art.

B.rationale: The passage says audiences valued artifice, not realism.

hints: What was the decree intended to do, and what did it help create?
candidates.remember: Conclusions often generalize from the passage's example.

candidates.stem: According to the last paragraph, one possible reason that animals sleep with both halves of the brain when it is safe is that doing so:

choices.A: may allow the brain to recover more efficiently.
choices.B: uses less energy than staying fully awake.
choices.C: lets them watch for predators in every direction.
choices.D: helps them remember where they have traveled.

candidates.evidence: sleeping with both halves allows the brain to recover more efficiently
candidates.explanation: The last paragraph offers one possibility: sleeping with both halves allows the brain to recover more efficiently.

B.rationale: The passage does not compare energy use.

C.rationale: Watching for predators is a reason for sleeping with half the brain, not both halves.

D.rationale: Memory of travel is not mentioned.

hints: What possibility does the last paragraph offer?

strategy.explanation: Locate "One possibility" in the last paragraph.

candidates.remember: Answer from the paragraph named in the question.
